stories.title: East Harlem Housing Proposal on City-Owned Lot Expands to 762 Units
stories.excerpt: An affordable and supportive housing complex slated for a city-owned site in Manhattan’s East Harlem neighborhood just got 62 units larger. The New York City Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD) submitted plans on Friday to rezone the city block surrounding 22 East 119th Street. The requested amendments will facilitate a housing project spanning three buildings with a total of 762 units. PincusCo first reported on the filing. The site is currently occupied by a six-story, 174-unit single room occupancy building where Volunteers of America–Greater New York hosts supportive housing for formerly homeless, single adults, many of whom are veterans. In accordance with a city policy that avoids “spot zoning” individual tax lots, the rezoning proposal would impact the entire East Harlem block, bounded by East 118th and East 119th streets, between Madison and Fifth avenues. In addition to the site’s designation as an urban renewal area and the disposition of city-owned property, HPD’s requested amendments would label the block as a Mandatory Inclusionary Housing area, ensuring affordable housing will be a part of any future redevelopments of the block’s privately owned buildings. A prior iteration of the project, sponsored by nonprofit Volunteers of America–Greater New York, planned 700 units across two buildings. Those included a 23-story supportive housing tower and a 25-story affordable housing tower. Plans also incorporated community space and commercial facilities for the nonprofit, with funding sought through HPD and the New York City Housing Development Corporation. Land use documents accompanying the newest proposal at 22 East 119th Street are not currently available. The change in site plans, and how surrounding buildings or project timelines will be impacted, is unclear. bullets: NYC HPD rezones East Harlem block for 762-unit affordable/supportive housing at 22 E. 119th St.
Project replaces 174-unit SRO; expands by 62 units via city block rezoning to avoid spot-zoning.
Affordable + supportive mix targets formerly homeless adults; preserves existing resident base.
stories.summary: New York City's Department of Housing Preservation and Development filed plans to rezone an East Harlem block bounded by East 118th–119th Streets and Madison–Fifth Avenues to enable a 762-unit affordable and supportive housing complex at 22 East 119th Street. The project will demolish the existing 174-unit SRO and replace it with three buildings. The rezoning strategy applies to the entire block to comply with city policy against spot-zoning individual tax lots.
stories.impact: Limited relevance to private multifamily development. This is public/non-profit affordable housing on city-owned land, competing for subsidy and financing outside market-rate underwriting. However, it signals sustained government commitment to affordable supply in Manhattan, which may pressure private developers in East Harlem to include affordability components or face entitlement friction. Watch for inclusionary zoning tightening in the submarket.

stories.title: Green Point Building 754K-SF Georgetown Spec Warehouse
stories.excerpt: Green Point Property plans to build a 754,000-square-foot spec building in Georgetown that could eventually have 3 million square feet of industrial space. It’s in the GTX Logistics Park at 1000 FM 972 The building costs are estimated at $42 million for the concrete tilt-wall warehouse shell that is scheduled to begin construction in October and be completed in November 2027. The Austin Business Journal reports the GTX Logistics Park is marketing 2.6 million square feet left on the 180 acres it still owns. Colliers International Group Inc.’s Travis Hicks and Chase Clancy handle leasing at the site. Georgetown is about 30 miles north of Austin with a population of nearly 107,000 people. Gree Point says its focus is on high-growth markets throughout Texas and the Southeastern US to acquire and develop industrial properties. Green Point’s team has 40 years of combined real estate investment experience and collectively has acquired, developed and managed real estate assets exceeding $3 billion across the United States. The post Green Point Building 754K-SF Georgetown Spec Warehouse appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Green Point Property breaks ground Oct. 2024 on 754K-SF spec warehouse in Georgetown, TX (near Austin).
Building cost $42M; part of 180-acre GTX Logistics Park with 2.6M SF remaining available.
Georgetown (30 mi. N of Austin) population 107K; Green Point targets high-growth TX & SE markets.
stories.summary: Green Point Property is constructing a 754,000-square-foot spec industrial warehouse at GTX Logistics Park in Georgetown, Texas, with an estimated cost of $42 million and completion slated for November 2027. The broader park spans 180 acres with 2.6 million square feet of leasing opportunity remaining. Green Point, which has acquired and developed over $3 billion in real estate assets, focuses on high-growth markets across Texas and the Southeast.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance to multifamily. Industrial spec development in Austin exurbs reflects logistics demand but does not directly affect apartment supply, demand, or capital allocation. However, continued industrial/logistics growth in Georgetown may support population and wage growth in outlying TX markets, potentially feeding demand for workforce housing in secondary submarkets; monitor for spillover demand into Fort Worth and surrounding rental markets.

stories.title: Truist Lends $277M on Jersey City Multifamily Tower Build
stories.excerpt: A joint venture between Rockpoint and Urby has secured $277 million of construction financing to develop the second phase of a multifamily tower in Jersey City, Commercial Observer has learned. Truist provided the loan for the sponsorship’s 748-unit 201 Hudson – by Urby project along the Jersey City waterfront. Rockpoint and Ubry joined forces to acquire land at 201 Hudson Street for the project in July, CO first reported at the time. “This financing reflects Truist’s continued commitment to supporting premier sponsors pursuing transformative multifamily developments in high-growth urban markets,” said Rebecca M. Cox, senior vice president and market manager at Truist National Real Estate. The transaction was led by Katie Kennedy, Northeast market leader at Truist, with Walt Reece, a director of real estate syndicated finance at Truist Securities, leading the syndication, according to the firm. Newmark negotiated the debt with a team consisting of Jordan Roeschlaub, Chris Kramer, Holden Witkoff and Jack Fenton. The brokerage firm also advised the joint venture partners on the joint venture capitalization with a team composed of Adam Spies, Adam Doneger and Michael Collins. Located in Jersey City’s Paulus Hook neighborhood, 201 Hudson – by Urby marks the second phase of a 69-story tower that will include 528,000 rentable square feet and 10,000 square feet of ground-floor retail space. Community amenities will include a pool, a fitness center and coworking spaces. Rockpoint, Urby and Newmark did not immediately return requests for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Truist funds $277M construction loan for Rockpoint/Urby 201 Hudson — 748-unit waterfront tower, Jersey City.
Joint venture acquired land July; Truist syndicated debt through Walt Reece (Truist Securities).
Urban waterfront multifamily in Gateway market signals capital appetite for Northeast high-density development.
stories.summary: Rockpoint and Urby secured $277 million of construction financing from Truist for 201 Hudson—a 748-unit multifamily tower in Jersey City's waterfront district. The joint venture acquired the land in July and is now moving into construction. Truist's Katie Kennedy led the deal, with syndication managed by Truist Securities, signaling strong lender confidence in the sponsor team and the project location.
stories.impact: Confirms robust capital availability for waterfront multifamily in Jersey City, a high-demand Gateway submarket with constrained land supply and strong renter migration from NYC. $277M construction debt on 748 units (~$370K per unit) reflects disciplined underwriting and active conduit lending. This reinforces Jersey City's status as a magnet for institutional capital and suggests developers should accelerate land acquisition in remaining waterfront and near-water parcels before cap rates compress further.

stories.title: Houston Office Building Owners Ink $250M Refi
stories.excerpt: PRP Real Assets and Riyad Capital secured a $250 million CMBS loan to refinance 777 Hidden Ridge, a 1.1 million-square-foot office property in Irving, Texas. Commercial Search reports that Bank of America originated the two-year, interest-only note with three one-year extension options. Previous debt includes a $253.8 million note issued by Citizens Financial Group in 2019, set to mature in 2029. KDC and Verizon completed the building in 2019, developed on a build-to-suit basis for Pioneer Natural Resources USA Inc. That same year, PRP and Riyad acquired the asset. Pioneer had inked a 20-year, triple-net lease set to run until 2039. The agreement has no early termination and no contractual rights for the remainder of the term. Pioneer has since left the building, but must fulfill the lease obligations. Pioneer is looking to sublease the space. The 10-story building has amenities such as a conference center, gym, coffee shop, on-site childcare, medical clinic and six-story parking garage with 2,569 spaces. The post Houston Office Building Owners Ink $250M Refi appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: PRP Real Assets & Riyad Capital refinance 1.1M-SF Irving office tower (777 Hidden Ridge) with $250M CMBS.
Bank of America originated 2-yr IO note; Pioneer Natural Resources tenant departed but remains liable on 20-yr lease through 2039.
Pioneer actively subletting; demonstrates office distress & sponsor leverage in energy-tenant dominated Irving market.
stories.summary: PRP Real Assets and Riyad Capital secured a $250 million CMBS refinance for 777 Hidden Ridge, a 1.1 million-square-foot office building in Irving, Texas. Bank of America provided a two-year interest-only note with three one-year extension options, replacing a 2019 Citizens Financial loan. The asset was developed in 2019 as a build-to-suit for Pioneer Natural Resources USA under a 20-year triple-net lease; Pioneer has since vacated but remains obligated through 2039 and is attempting to sublease the space.
stories.impact: Illustrates office sector stress in Texas energy hubs and refinancing pressure as triple-net anchors default on occupancy. However, not directly material to multifamily development. Monitor Irving/Dallas office weakness as signal of regional employment volatility—energy sector layoffs could suppress wage growth and renter creditworthiness in DFW metro, pressuring rent growth even in healthy apartment corridors.

stories.title: VIC Partners Obtains Construction Loan for 268-Unit FW Workforce Rental Community
stories.excerpt: VIC Partners obtained a $36.5 million primary line of credit for the construction of Vic Centre, a 268-unit workforce-housing development at 7120 Anderson Blvd. in Fort Worth outside of Loop 820 and north of Interstate 30. The project is being developed by Vic Partners and M-13 Construction. OakNorth Bank will provide the loan as part of a $48 million joint financing with Hickory CRE Capital, a commercial real estate lender. Concord Summit Capital arranged the construction loan. VIC suggests the cost of the construction will be $41.7 million. The development will consist of nine three-story residential buildings, a clubhouse, fitness center, pickleball court and business center along with 402 parking spaces.  The post VIC Partners Obtains Construction Loan for 268-Unit FW Workforce Rental Community appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: VIC Partners finances 268-unit Vic Centre (Fort Worth Loop 820 corridor) with $36.5M + $48M joint construction loan.
OakNorth Bank & Hickory CRE Capital fund $41.7M project cost; M-13 Construction develops nine 3-story buildings.
Workforce-housing targeting outside Loop 820 indicates supply pressure in core FW and developer pivot to secondary corridors.
stories.summary: VIC Partners and M-13 Construction secured $48 million in construction financing (OakNorth Bank and Hickory CRE Capital) for Vic Centre, a 268-unit workforce-housing development at 7120 Anderson Boulevard in Fort Worth outside Loop 820. The project cost is estimated at $41.7 million and will comprise nine three-story residential buildings with amenities including clubhouse, fitness center, and pickleball court.
stories.impact: Workforce housing construction in Fort Worth exurban/secondary locations signals reduced appetite for urban-core development—likely due to supply saturation in core FW submarkets and rent concessions. The 268-unit garden-style format outside Loop 820 suggests developers are targeting affordability-constrained renters in peripheral areas. This trend weakens urban submarket fundamentals and may extend absorption timelines; institutional capital flowing to secondary sites could reduce land values in prime FW corridors in the medium term.

stories.title: W Properties Mixing BTR and Garden-Style Apartments in Melissa
stories.excerpt: W Properties plans to build a 252-unit garden-style multifamily community on approximately 12 acres adjacent to Everbloom (shown), the company’s 343-unit build-to-rent community in Melissa, Texas. The company said it’s taking a different approach with garden-style apartments, a sector still working through elevated supply and concessions across North Texas. Texas multifamily permitting across its five major metros has fallen by more than half from its 2023 peak, while Dallas-Fort Worth continues to absorb a significant pipeline of apartments already under construction. W Properties Andrew Welker added, “BTR and garden-style apartments are different products, and we would not have started a garden-style project in that same environment. We expect to go vertical by mid-2027, positioning this community for an early 2029 leasing season, when we believe today’s supply pressure will look materially different.” The post W Properties Mixing BTR and Garden-Style Apartments in Melissa appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: W Properties plans 252-unit garden-style community in Melissa (DFW suburbs), adjacent to existing 343-unit BTR.
Vertical start target: mid-2027; lease-up: early 2029 (18-month delay). TX permitting fell 50%+ from 2023 peak.
Developer explicitly timing garden-style for market normalization, expects 'materially different' supply environment by 2029.
stories.summary: W Properties is developing a 252-unit garden-style multifamily community on 12 acres in Melissa, Texas, adjacent to its existing 343-unit build-to-rent community Everbloom. The developer plans to begin vertical construction in mid-2027 with leasing commencing in early 2029. W Properties acknowledged that Texas multifamily permitting across its five major metros has fallen more than 50% from its 2023 peak, and the company is intentionally timing the garden-style delivery for when supply pressure is expected to ease.
stories.impact: Critical signal: developer deliberately delaying lease-up to early 2029 to avoid today's concession environment and position for healthier absorption. Texas multifamily permitting collapse (down >50% YoY) confirms supply normalization is underway, but pipeline absorption will take 18–24 months. This suggests DFW rents will remain under pressure through 2027, cap rates may stay elevated, and only projects with strong equity cushions or long hold periods will pencil. Developers should prioritize land control in Melissa/North Dallas corridor ahead of 2027 construction starts, when demand recovery becomes visible.

stories.title: REITs Post Record High FFO in Q2 2026: Nareit
stories.excerpt: REITs posted record highs for funds from operations (FFO) and net operating income (NOI) in 2026’s second quarter while maintaining strong balance sheets, according to Nareit’s latest REIT Industry Tracker. More than 70% of REITs reported year-over-year increases in FFO, while nearly 80% reported year-over-year increases in NOI. Industry Tracker data show that FFO reached $22.4 billion in Q2, up 12.4% Y-O-Y. Meanwhile, NOI reached $32.7 billion, up 6.8%. Additionally, same-store NOI experienced a 4.1% Y-O-Y gain, demonstrating that REIT operations outpaced inflation in the second quarter, which was 3.5% “The strength we’re seeing from the REIT industry isn’t coming from one measure or sector,” said John Worth, EVP of research & investor outreach at Nareit. “Across the board, REITs continue to generate strong income from their properties reflecting rising occupancy while maintaining robust balance sheets. That combination speaks to the underlying resilience of the industry amid ongoing economic uncertainty.” The post REITs Post Record High FFO in Q2 2026: Nareit appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Nareit: REITs posted record FFO ($22.4B, +12.4% YoY) and NOI ($32.7B, +6.8% YoY) in Q2 2026.
70%+ of REITs reported FFO gains; 80%+ reported NOI gains; same-store NOI +4.1% YoY, outpaced 3.5% inflation.
Strong occupancy & balance sheets amid 'ongoing economic uncertainty'; broad-based sector strength.
stories.summary: REITs reported record-high funds from operations and net operating income in the second quarter of 2026, according to Nareit's Industry Tracker. FFO reached $22.4 billion, up 12.4% year-over-year, while NOI hit $32.7 billion, up 6.8%. More than 70% of REITs posted FFO increases and nearly 80% reported NOI gains. Same-store NOI grew 4.1% year-over-year, outpacing the 3.5% inflation rate, demonstrating operational resilience.
stories.impact: Macro validation of strong REIT fundamentals in 2026, signaling investor confidence and capital availability for multifamily operators and development. Record FFO/NOI and improving same-store metrics suggest rents are recovering, occupancy is climbing, and debt refinancing conditions are normalizing. This supports development underwriting assumptions in gateway/tier-1 markets and validates 2027–2028 lease-up timing for projects in healthy submarkets (e.g., Jersey City, Austin, DFW). However, broad gains mask regional variation; developers must stress-test against DFW concession environment and watch for slowdown in oversupplied markets.

stories.title: Mamdani Sets Sights on Fixing — Not Replacing — Deteriorating Section of BQE
stories.excerpt: Will Mayor Zohran Mamdani be the first administration to finally fix the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway (BQE) along Brooklyn Heights? Mamdani announced Monday morning that the New York City Department of Transportation (DOT) would build bypasses around the surrounding neighborhoods and maintain access to local attractions while finally rebuilding the swiftly deteriorating cantilever portion of the freeway. DOT would build a two-level bypass above Furman Street from Atlantic Avenue to Columbia Heights, sitting below the promenade and not extending above the current highway. The city would also create a second elevated bypass from Columbia Heights to the Manhattan Bridge. The Mamdani administration plans to start the estimated $4 billion project in 2030, despite a sense of urgency from officials. The city estimates the project could take 10 years. The Mamdani administration said it believes this renovation, as opposed to a replacement, will extend the life of the BQE for another 40 years. “After decades of kicking the can down the road and indecision that failed to yield substantial results, we will act with urgency to rehabilitate the city’s portion of the BQE to ensure the safety of New Yorkers and minimize the likelihood of massive traffic diversions into Brooklyn neighborhoods,” DOT Commissioner Mike Flynn said in a statement. “While the city and the state must right the wrongs of Robert Moses with the BQE and other infrastructure plowed through urban communities, decades of political paralysis have left us out of options.” For every year that the city procrastinates, costs increase by an estimated $160 million, according to the announcement. “For decades, prior administrations have failed to deliver urgent long-term repairs to BQE Central — but we can no longer afford to wait for the perfect solution,” Mamdani said in a statement. “We’re going to fix the aging concrete, repair the deteriorating triple cantilever and build temporary roads that keep the highway operabl
bullets: NYC DOT & Mayor Mamdani plan $4B BQE repair (not replacement) starting 2030; 10-year timeline.
Two-level bypass above Furman St. (Atlantic to Columbia Heights); second elevated bypass Columbia Heights to Manhattan Bridge.
Repair extends BQE life 40 years; represents major infrastructure commitment to Brooklyn waterfront access & viability.
stories.summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced that the Department of Transportation will repair (rather than replace) the deteriorating cantilever section of the Brooklyn-Queens Expressway, with construction beginning in 2030 and expected to take 10 years at an estimated cost of $4 billion. The plan includes two-level bypasses above Furman Street and a second elevated section from Columbia Heights to the Manhattan Bridge, designed to extend the highway's life another 40 years.
stories.impact: Indirect but important for Brooklyn waterfront multifamily development. A decade-long BQE reconstruction starting 2030 will create construction chaos, noise, and access friction for Brooklyn Heights, Dumbo, and waterfront residential assets. Developers should avoid major lease-ups or Phase II projects directly adjacent to the BQE corridor during 2030–2040. However, the city's commitment to long-term BQE viability validates waterfront residential fundamentals and suggests Brooklyn will remain a desirable rental market; frontload construction now (2026–2029) to avoid 2030+ disruption.

stories.title: Kinsmen Property Group Plans to Bring 322 New Homes to 156-166 Bowery
stories.excerpt: Kinsmen Property Group, a New York City-based real estate development and investment firm, has big plans to build 322 homes along the Bowery in Manhattan’s Nolita neighborhood, Commercial Observer has learned. After previously filing plans to demolish a 15,000-square-foot set of vacant buildings at 156-166 Bowery in October 2024, Kinsmen has now filed a land use application with the Department of City Planning to transform the now-vacant lot into three mixed-use, mixed-income buildings with a total of 322 homes, according to the firm. If approved, the three buildings would comprise a 29-story building with 124 affordable apartments for seniors; a 26-story building with 99 mixed-income units and 3,260 square feet of ground-floor retail space; and another 26-story building with 99 mixed-income units and 4,391 square feet of ground-floor retail space. The project, which would be designed by architects Kohn Pedersen Fox and Beyer Blinder Belle, is expected to enter public review through a Uniform Land Use Review Procedure (ULURP) by the end of the year. “We are excited to bring more than 300 new homes to Lower Manhattan at a time when housing is urgently needed across the city,” Ari Zagdanski, principal of Kinsmen, said in a statement. “This project is designed to honor the rich history of the Bowery while also addressing the city’s housing needs head-on.” The site at 156-166 Bowery has already been through various different planned projects. In 2022, previous owner Real Estate Equities Corporation (REEC) — which had signed a 99-year ground lease for the properties in 2020 for $50 million — filed plans to construct a seven-story, 73,000-square-foot retail and office building on the site. Construction on that project eventually stalled. It’s unclear whether REEC still owns the ground lease at the Nolita site, which Kinsmen bought in a set of separate purchases in 2016 and 2017 for a total of $53.5 million, according to records. bullets: Kinsmen Property Group plans 322 homes across 3 mixed-use towers at 156–166 Bowery (Nolita), Manhattan.
29-story building: 124 affordable senior units; two 26-story towers: 99 mixed-income units each + ground retail.
Land use app filed; ULURP review expected by end of year. Architects: Kohn Pedersen Fox, Beyer Blinder Belle.
stories.summary: Kinsmen Property Group filed a land use application to develop 322 homes across three mixed-use buildings on the Bowery in Manhattan's Nolita neighborhood, replacing 15,000 square feet of vacant structures. The project comprises a 29-story building with 124 affordable apartments for seniors, and two 26-story buildings with 99 mixed-income units each and ground-floor retail (3,260 and 4,391 square feet respectively). The project, designed by KPF and Beyer Blinder Belle, is expected to enter Uniform Land Use Review Procedure (ULURP) by year-end.
stories.impact: Signals continued institutional appetite for mixed-income, mixed-use multifamily in Manhattan's secondary neighborhoods (Nolita). The inclusion of 124 senior affordable units suggests affordability pressure or inclusionary zoning leverage in the application. Developers should monitor ULURP timing and approval contingencies; if approved, it validates Bowery/Nolita as developable corridor and may trigger land assemblies nearby. Affordable senior component may require LIHTC or HUD financing, adding complexity and timeline; not a pure market-rate play.

stories.title: Circle Realty Secures 38K SF of New Leases at 14 Penn Plaza
stories.excerpt: Circle Realty Group has closed on 37,600 square feet of new leases in Midtown, Commercial Observer has learned. The two largest deals at 225 West 34th Street, also known as 14 Penn Plaza, were for civil engineering company Bohler Engineering, which expanded from 8,000 square feet to 14,000 square feet, and cybersecurity firm T&M USA, which took 14,000 square feet, according to Circle Realty. Bohler signed a 10-year lease and asking rent in the building was $67 per square foot. The length of T&M’s lease was unclear. “These tenants came to me because we’re at the center of transportation and we have a first-class property,” Circle Realty President Jay Futersak told CO. “Tenants know that what we promised is what we deliver.” Futersak represented his own firm in-house and both tenants in the deals. Smaller recent deals in the building were for accounting and advisory firm Calibre CPA Group, which signed a 10-year, 6,100-square-foot lease and is relocating from 462 Seventh Avenue. Mark Furst and Benjamin Saftler of Kaufman Leasing, the brokerage arm of the Kaufman Organization, handled the deal for the Washington, D.C.-based accounting firm and did not immediately comment. Meanwhile, discrimination law firm Fitapelli & Schaffer is also relocating from 20 Liberty Street to 14 Penn with a new 3,514-square-foot lease. Robert Gallucci of Colliers negotiated on behalf of the law firm and did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Futersak repped ownership in-house in the Calibre and Fitapelli deals. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Circle Realty leases 37.6K SF at 14 Penn Plaza (225 W 34th, Midtown) to Bohler Engineering & T&M USA.
Bohler expanded 8K to 14K SF (10-yr lease, $67/SF asking); T&M USA took 14K SF; Calibre CPA 6.1K SF.
Office leasing activity in Midtown reflects selective tenant demand for transit-accessible, Class-A assets.
stories.summary: Circle Realty Group closed 37,600 square feet of new leases at 14 Penn Plaza (225 West 34th Street) in Midtown Manhattan. Civil engineering firm Bohler Engineering expanded from 8,000 to 14,000 square feet on a 10-year lease at $67 per square foot, while cybersecurity firm T&M USA leased 14,000 square feet. Accounting firm Calibre CPA Group signed a 10-year, 6,100-square-foot lease. Circle Realty President Jay Futersak cited the building's transit access and first-class quality as drivers of tenant demand.
stories.impact: Minimal relevance to multifamily development. However, office leasing momentum at Midtown Class-A, transit-rich buildings signals selective recovery in NYC office—tech and professional services tenants remain viable. This may support residential demand from young professional renters in Manhattan and Gateway; conversely, if office continues to normalize, it could reduce local job density and rent growth in Midtown-adjacent residential markets. Multifamily developers should monitor office absorption trends in Midtown/Hudson Yards as leading indicators of wage/employment stability in NYC.
